theory_refs.why: Turns n into a target complexity before you think of an idea.

theory_refs.at: ↳ Bottleneck: the inner loop re-adds a[0..i−1]
theory_refs.why: Shows exactly why re-adding the prefix is wasted work — the move this whole problem is about.
The running-total template your pseudocode follows line by line.

theory_refs.at: Time O(n): one loop, O(1) work inside
theory_refs.why: How "one loop with O(1) inside" becomes O(n).

theory_refs.at: "This output array is called a prefix sum array"
theory_refs.why: The same array answers any range sum on Day 4 — read it then, or peek now.

problems.note:
1. Problem
   • out[i] = a[0] + … + a[i]  (Running Sum, LC 1480)
2. Pattern: running state
   • Trigger: answer at i = answer at i−1 + one change
3. Brute → optimal
   • Brute: for each i, add a[0..i] again → O(n²)
       ◦ Bottleneck: re-adding a prefix the last step already added
   • Optimal: keep `run`, add a[i], write it → O(n)
4. Pseudocode
   • STATE run = 0 · LOOP i = 0..n−1 · UPDATE run += a[i]; out[i] = run · RETURN out
5. Remember
   • This output is a **prefix sum array** (Day 4 uses it for range sums)
   • O(1) extra space: a[i] += a[i−1] in place
✎ In my words: ______________________________________________

stages.title: Understand
stages.body:
✍️ f(array a of n ints) → array out where out[i] = a[0] + a[1] + … + a[i].
- Constraints: n ≤ 1000, values between −10⁶ and 10⁶. Even O(n²) passes, but the point is to see the O(n) idea.
- Example: [1, 2, 3, 4] → [1, 3, 6, 10].

stages.title: Analyse
stages.body:
✍️ By hand on [3, 1, 2]: out[0] = 3. For out[1] I wrote 3 + 1 — but I did not re-add 3, I took out[0] and added 1. For out[2] I took out[1] = 4 and added 2 → 6.
✍️ Hard part: none really — the trap is writing two loops because the definition "sum of a[0..i]" sounds like a loop.
✍️ Edges: one element → itself. Negatives are fine.

stages.title: Brainstorm: brute → optimal
stages.body:
✍️ **1. Brute.** For each i, loop j from 0 to i and add a[j]. O(n²) time, O(1) extra.
✍️ ↳ Bottleneck: the inner loop re-adds a[0..i−1], which the previous iteration already added.
✍️ ↳ Unlock question: "Am I recomputing something that only changed a little?" ([[meta-bottleneck-method#unlock-questions]]) — yes, by exactly one element.
>> detour meta-bottleneck-method#unlock-questions | The seven unlock questions — you will reuse them all month | 2 min
✍️ **2. Optimal.** Keep the previous total and add a[i]. O(n) time.
✍️ (Bonus: write into `a` itself — `a[i] += a[i−1]` — for O(1) extra space.)

stages.title: Algorithm in words
stages.body:
✍️ 1. Start a running total at 0.
✍️ 2. For each element from left to right, add it to the running total.
✍️ 3. Write the running total into the output at that position.
✍️ 4. Return the output.

stages.title: Pseudocode
stages.body:
```
STATE   run = 0;  out = array of size n
LOOP    for i in 0..n-1
UPDATE    run = run + a[i]
          out[i] = run
RETURN  out
```

stages.title: Reference C++
Edge cases and complexity
stages.body:
✍️ Time O(n): one loop, O(1) work inside. Space O(n) for the output (O(1) extra if you overwrite the input).
- Overflow: 1000 × 10⁶ = 10⁹ fits in int. In general prefix sums need `long long` ([[cpp-integer-overflow#where]]).
- One element → [a[0]].

stages.title: Carry forward
stages.body:
✍️ "Answer at i depends on the answer at i−1" → keep it in a variable, do not loop back.
✍️ This output array is called a **prefix sum array**. On Day 4 it answers any range sum in O(1).

stages.title: Interview follow-ups
stages.body:
- *Can you do it in O(1) extra space?* Overwrite: `for i in 1..n−1: a[i] += a[i−1]`.
- *Now answer many "sum from l to r" queries.* Build the prefix array once with a leading 0, answer `pre[r+1] − pre[l]` ([[ps-prefix-sum-basics#template]]).

siblings.title: Find Pivot Index
siblings.maps: Same running total, but now you compare "sum to my left" with "sum to my right" = total − left − a[i].
siblings.note:
• Pivot: sum left of i == sum right of i
• right = total − left − a[i] → one pass with running `left`
• CHECK before adding a[i] to left · O(n), O(1)

stages.title: Analyse
stages.body:
✍️ Find the leftmost index i where (sum of elements left of i) equals (sum of elements right of i); −1 if none.
✍️ Brute force: for every i, add up both sides → O(n²).

stages.title: Brainstorm
stages.body:
✍️ Bottleneck: re-adding both sides for every i.
✍️ Fix: the total is fixed. Keep `left` as running state; then right = total − left − a[i] in O(1). → O(n).

stages.title: Algorithm in words
stages.body: ✍️ 1. Compute the total sum. 2. Walk i from left to right with `left = 0`. 3. If left == total − left − a[i], return i. 4. Add a[i] to left. 5. Return −1.

stages.title: Pseudocode
stages.body:
```
STATE   total = sum(a); left = 0
LOOP    for i in 0..n-1
CHECK     if left == total - left - a[i]: return i
UPDATE    left += a[i]          (after the check: a[i] is not on its own left)
RETURN  -1
```

stages.title: Reference C++
Quick theory
stages.body:
✍️ "Left part vs right part" problems = prefix sum + total. See [[ps-prefix-sum-basics#variations]].
- Same CHECK-then-UPDATE ordering lesson as Two Sum tomorrow.

siblings.title: Left and Right Sum Differences
siblings.maps: Output |leftSum − rightSum| at every index — the pivot-index idea, but recorded everywhere.

stages.title: Brainstorm
stages.body: ✍️ Brute O(n²) → running `left` + total → O(n).

stages.title: Algorithm in words
stages.body: ✍️ Total first; walk with left; right = total − left − a[i]; store the absolute difference; add a[i] to left.

stages.title: Pseudocode
stages.body:
```
total = sum(a); left = 0
for i in 0..n-1: out[i] = |left - (total - left - a[i])|; left += a[i]
```

stages.title: Reference C++
Quick theory
stages.body: ✍️ Any "left vs right of i" quantity = one running prefix + one total.

siblings.title: Minimum Value to Get Positive Step by Step Sum
siblings.maps: Running sum again; the answer depends on the lowest point the running sum ever reaches.

stages.title: Analyse
stages.body: ✍️ Choose the smallest positive start value so that start + running sum is ≥ 1 at every step.

stages.title: Brainstorm
stages.body:
✍️ Brute: try start = 1, 2, 3, … and simulate → O(n · answer).
✍️ Observation: only the **minimum** prefix sum matters. Need start + minPrefix ≥ 1 → start = max(1, 1 − minPrefix). O(n).

stages.title: Algorithm in words
stages.body: ✍️ Track the running sum and its minimum; answer = max(1, 1 − minimum).

stages.title: Pseudocode
Reference C++
Quick theory
stages.body: ✍️ "Must stay positive / never drop below" → track the minimum of the running sum, not every step.

theory_refs.why: Why updating best only on a reset misses a streak that runs to the end.
Day 5 turns this exact problem into "flip at most k zeros".

problems.note:
1. Problem
   • Longest block of consecutive 1s (LC 485)
2. Pattern: running state — streak that resets
3. Brute → optimal
   • Brute: count forward from every start → O(n²)
       ◦ Bottleneck: a block is recounted from each of its positions
   • Optimal: cur = (x == 1) ? cur + 1 : 0; best = max(best, cur) → O(n), O(1)
4. Pitfalls
   • Update best **every** step — a streak can end at the last element
5. Leads to
   • "Flip at most k zeros" = Day 5 sliding window (Max Consecutive Ones III)
✎ In my words: ______________________________________________

stages.title: Understand
stages.body:
✍️ f(binary array) → length of the longest block of consecutive 1s.
- n ≤ 10⁵ → need O(n) (or O(n log n)).
- Example: [1,1,0,1,1,1] → 3.

stages.title: Analyse
stages.body:
✍️ By hand: I count 1, 2 — hit a 0, reset to 0 — then 1, 2, 3. The answer is the biggest count I said.
✍️ Hard part: remembering the best while the current count keeps resetting.
✍️ Edges: all zeros → 0; all ones → n; the longest block at the very end.

stages.title: Brainstorm: brute → optimal
stages.body:
✍️ **1. Brute.** From every start i, count forward while 1s continue. O(n²) on an all-ones array.
✍️ ↳ Bottleneck: a block of length L is re-counted from each of its L positions.
✍️ ↳ Unlock: "recomputing something that only changed a little" — the streak ending at i is (streak ending at i−1) + 1, or 0.
✍️ **2. Optimal.** One pass with `cur` (streak ending here) and `best`. O(n), O(1).

stages.title: Algorithm in words
stages.body:
✍️ 1. Keep a current streak and a best streak, both 0.
✍️ 2. For each element: if it is 1, extend the current streak; otherwise reset it to 0.
✍️ 3. After each element, update best with the current streak.
✍️ 4. Return best.

stages.title: Pseudocode
stages.body:
```
STATE   cur = 0; best = 0
LOOP    for x in a
UPDATE    if x == 1: cur = cur + 1  else: cur = 0
          best = max(best, cur)          (every step, not only on a reset)
RETURN  best
```

stages.title: Reference C++
Edge cases and complexity
stages.body:
✍️ O(n) time, O(1) space.
✍️ If `best` were updated only when a 0 appears, [1,1,1] would return 0. Update every step.
- All zeros → best stays 0.

stages.title: Carry forward
stages.body:
✍️ "Streak / consecutive" → current + best; reset on break; update best every iteration.
✍️ When the problem lets you break the rule up to k times, the streak becomes a **sliding window** (Day 5).

stages.title: Interview follow-ups
stages.body:
- *You may flip at most one 0.* (LeetCode 487) Track the streak before and after the last zero, or a window with ≤ 1 zero.
- *At most k flips.* Variable window with a zero budget ([[sw-variable-window#budget]]).
- *Data arrives as a stream.* The same two variables work — nothing needs to be stored.

siblings.title: Consecutive Characters
siblings.maps: Same streak, but "matching" means "equal to the previous character" instead of "equal to 1".
siblings.note:
• Streak of equal neighbours: extend if s[i] == s[i−1]
• Reset to **1** (the current char is a run) · O(n)

stages.title: Analyse
stages.body: ✍️ Longest substring made of one repeated character. "abbcccddddeeeeedcba" → 5.

stages.title: Brainstorm
stages.body: ✍️ Brute: from each start count equal characters → O(n²). Optimal: streak that extends when s[i] == s[i−1], resets to **1** (not 0) otherwise — the current character alone is a run.

stages.title: Algorithm in words
stages.body: ✍️ cur = best = 1; for i from 1: extend if equal to previous else cur = 1; best = max.

stages.title: Pseudocode
stages.body:
```
cur = 1; best = 1
for i in 1..n-1:
    cur = (s[i] == s[i-1]) ? cur + 1 : 1
    best = max(best, cur)
return best
```

stages.title: Reference C++
Quick theory
stages.body: ✍️ Reset value depends on meaning: "count of matching elements" resets to 0; "length of a run that includes me" resets to 1 ([[arr-single-pass-running-state#pitfalls]]).

stages.title: Analyse
stages.body: ✍️ Longest strictly increasing **contiguous** run.

stages.title: Brainstorm
stages.body: ✍️ Same streak; extend when a[i] > a[i−1], else reset to 1. (Non-contiguous version is LIS, Day 28.)

stages.title: Algorithm in words
stages.body: ✍️ cur = best = 1; extend or reset; track best.

stages.title: Pseudocode
stages.body:
```
cur = best = 1
for i in 1..n-1: cur = a[i] > a[i-1] ? cur+1 : 1; best = max(best, cur)
```

stages.title: Reference C++
Quick theory
stages.body: ✍️ "Continuous" = contiguous = streak. "Subsequence" without "continuous" = DP ([[dp-lis]]).

siblings.title: Length of the Longest Alphabetical Continuous Substring
siblings.maps: Streak condition "s[i] is exactly the next letter after s[i−1]".

stages.title: Analyse
stages.body: ✍️ Longest substring like "abc", "xyz" where each letter is the next in the alphabet.

stages.title: Brainstorm
stages.body: ✍️ Same streak with condition `s[i] − s[i−1] == 1`. O(n).

stages.title: Algorithm in words
stages.body: ✍️ Extend when consecutive letters, else reset to 1; track the best.

stages.title: Pseudocode
stages.body:
```
cur = best = 1
for i in 1..n-1: cur = (s[i]-s[i-1] == 1) ? cur+1 : 1; best = max(best, cur)
```

stages.title: Reference C++
Quick theory
stages.body: ✍️ Character arithmetic `s[i] − s[i−1]` ([[cpp-string#basics]]).

theory_refs.at: "in place", keep the order of non-zeros
theory_refs.why: The trigger words that point to the read/write pointer.

theory_refs.at: ↳ Bottleneck of B: elements are shifted again and again
theory_refs.why: Why erase-and-shift is O(n²) and how moving each element once fixes it.
Why this problem needs swap (or a fill pass) instead of a plain copy.

problems.note:
1. Problem
   • Move all 0s to the end, keep the order of the rest, in place (LC 283)
2. Pattern: read / write pointer
   • Trigger: "in-place", "keep relative order"
3. Brute → optimal
   • Brute A: new array → O(n) space ✗ · Brute B: erase + push_back → O(n²)
       ◦ Bottleneck: the same elements get shifted again and again
   • Optimal: move each non-zero once, to index `write` → O(n), O(1)
4. Pseudocode
   • write = 0 · for read: if a[read] ≠ 0 → swap(a[write], a[read]); write++
5. Remember
   • **Swap**, not copy — the zeros must survive at the back
   • Invariant: a[0..write−1] = non-zeros in order
✎ In my words: ______________________________________________

stages.title: Understand
stages.body:
✍️ f(array, modified in place) → all non-zero elements first in their original order, then all zeros.
- n ≤ 10⁴. Must not copy the array.
- Example: [0,1,0,3,12] → [1,3,12,0,0].
>> detour cx-space-and-in-place#in-place | What "in place" allows and forbids | 2 min

stages.title: Analyse
stages.body:
✍️ By hand: I look at each non-zero and slide it to "the next free spot at the front". The free spot starts at 0 and moves one step each time I place something.
✍️ Hard part: doing it without a second array, and without disturbing the order of non-zeros.
✍️ Edges: no zeros (nothing moves), all zeros, a single element.

stages.title: Brainstorm: brute → optimal
stages.body:
✍️ **1. Brute A.** Copy non-zeros into a new array, pad with zeros, copy back. O(n) time but O(n) space — breaks "in place".
✍️ **1. Brute B.** When you see a 0, erase it and push a 0 at the end. Erase shifts the whole tail → O(n) per zero → O(n²).
✍️ ↳ Bottleneck of B: the same elements are shifted again and again.
✍️ ↳ Unlock: each kept element has a known final position = number of kept elements before it. Move it there **once**.
✍️ **2. Optimal.** Read pointer visits everything; write pointer = next free spot. Swap a non-zero into the write spot. O(n), O(1).

stages.title: Algorithm in words
stages.body:
✍️ 1. Set the write position to 0.
✍️ 2. For each read position from left to right: if the element is non-zero, swap it with the element at the write position and advance the write position.
✍️ 3. Zeros end up behind, because every swap pushes a zero (or the same element) backwards.

stages.title: Pseudocode
stages.body:
```
STATE   write = 0
LOOP    for read in 0..n-1
CHECK     if a[read] != 0
UPDATE      swap(a[write], a[read]); write = write + 1
RETURN  (array modified in place)
```

stages.title: Reference C++
Edge cases and complexity
stages.body:
✍️ O(n) time (one pass), O(1) extra space.
✍️ Invariant: a[0..write−1] holds the non-zeros seen so far in order; a[write..read−1] are all zeros.
- When there are no zeros, `write == read` and every swap is with itself — harmless.

stages.title: Carry forward
stages.body:
✍️ "In place, keep order, remove/move some elements" → read/write pointer. The only problem-specific line is `keep(a[read])`.
✍️ Use **swap** when the removed elements must still be in the array; **copy** when what is left after `write` does not matter.

stages.title: Interview follow-ups
stages.body:
- *Minimise the number of writes.* Copy non-zeros forward, then fill the tail with zeros only where needed; or skip the swap when read == write.
- *Move all zeros to the front instead.* Walk from the right with the write pointer at n−1.
- *Partition evens before odds.* Same template with keep = "is even" (LeetCode 905).

siblings.title: Remove Element
siblings.maps: keep = "a[read] != val", and copy is enough because the tail does not matter.
siblings.note:
• Read/write with keep = a[read] ≠ val
• Copy is enough (tail doesn't matter) · return write

stages.title: Analyse
stages.body: ✍️ Remove every occurrence of `val` in place; return k = number of remaining elements, which must be in a[0..k−1].

stages.title: Brainstorm
stages.body: ✍️ Brute: erase each match → O(n²). Optimal: read/write pointer with copy → O(n), O(1).

stages.title: Algorithm in words
stages.body: ✍️ write = 0; for each element not equal to val, copy it to a[write] and advance write; return write.

stages.title: Pseudocode
stages.body:
```
write = 0
for read in 0..n-1:
    if a[read] != val: a[write] = a[read]; write++
return write
```

stages.title: Reference C++
Quick theory
stages.body: ✍️ The same template as Move Zeroes; copy instead of swap because only a[0..k−1] is checked ([[arr-read-write-pointer#swap-vs-copy]]).

siblings.title: Sort Array By Parity
siblings.maps: keep = "is even", with swap so the odds survive at the back.

stages.title: Analyse
stages.body: ✍️ Return the array with all evens before all odds (any order within each group).

stages.title: Brainstorm
stages.body: ✍️ Two new arrays → O(n) space. In place: read/write pointer with swap, keep = even. (Two pointers from both ends also works.)

stages.title: Algorithm in words
stages.body: ✍️ For each element that is even, swap it into a[write] and advance write.

stages.title: Pseudocode
stages.body:
```
write = 0
for read in 0..n-1: if a[read] % 2 == 0: swap(a[write], a[read]); write++
return a
```

stages.title: Reference C++
Quick theory
stages.body: ✍️ Two-group partition = read/write + swap. Three groups = Dutch flag ([[sort-dutch-national-flag]]).

siblings.title: Apply Operations to an Array
siblings.maps: A simulation pass, then exactly Move Zeroes.

stages.title: Analyse
stages.body: ✍️ For i = 0..n−2: if a[i] == a[i+1], double a[i] and set a[i+1] = 0. Then shift all zeros to the end.

stages.title: Brainstorm
stages.body: ✍️ Two passes: the simulation (O(n)), then the read/write pointer (O(n)).

stages.title: Algorithm in words
stages.body: ✍️ Run the merge rule left to right; then move non-zeros to the front keeping order.

stages.title: Pseudocode
stages.body:
```
for i in 0..n-2: if a[i] == a[i+1]: a[i] *= 2; a[i+1] = 0
write = 0; for read: if a[read] != 0: swap(a[write++], a[read])
```

stages.title: Reference C++
Quick theory
stages.body: ✍️ OA problems often chain an easy simulation with a known pattern; spot the known part and reuse its template.

theory_refs.at: "because it is sorted, a value is new when it differs from the last kept"
theory_refs.why: Sortedness turns "seen before?" into a neighbour comparison.
The keep-rule table, including this exact rule.
Why `a[write−k]` generalises to "keep at most k copies" (the must-study sibling).

problems.note:
1. Problem
   • Sorted array → keep one copy of each value in front, return k (LC 26)
2. Pattern: read / write pointer + sortedness
   • Sorted ⇒ duplicates are adjacent ⇒ "new?" = differs from last kept
3. Brute → optimal
   • Brute: set of seen values → O(n) space
       ◦ Waste: the set answers a question sortedness already answers
   • Optimal: keep if a[read] ≠ a[write−1] → O(n), O(1)
4. Pseudocode
   • write = 1 · for read = 1..n−1: if a[read] ≠ a[write−1] → a[write++] = a[read] · return write
5. Remember
   • Compare with the **written** array: "at most k copies" → a[write−k]
✎ In my words: ______________________________________________

stages.title: Understand
stages.body:
✍️ f(sorted array, in place) → k = number of distinct values; the first k slots must hold them in order.
- n ≤ 3·10⁴, sorted non-decreasing.
- Example: [0,0,1,1,1,2,2,3,3,4] → k = 5, front = [0,1,2,3,4].

stages.title: Analyse
stages.body:
✍️ By hand: because it is sorted, a value is "new" exactly when it differs from the last value I kept.
✍️ Hard part: deciding what to compare against — the previous element in the input, or the last kept element. (For this problem both work; for the "keep two" version only the kept one does.)
✍️ Edges: one element → k = 1; all equal → k = 1.

stages.title: Brainstorm: brute → optimal
stages.body:
✍️ **1. Brute.** Use a set to collect distinct values, write them back sorted. O(n log n) or O(n) time, O(n) space.
✍️ ↳ Bottleneck: the set exists only to answer "have I seen this?", but sortedness already answers that in O(1).
✍️ **2. Optimal.** Read/write pointer; keep a[read] if it differs from a[write−1]. O(n), O(1).

stages.title: Algorithm in words
stages.body:
✍️ 1. The first element is always kept: write = 1.
✍️ 2. For each later element, if it differs from the last kept element a[write−1], copy it to a[write] and advance.
✍️ 3. Return write.

stages.title: Pseudocode
stages.body:
```
STATE   write = 1                         (n ≥ 1 is guaranteed)
LOOP    for read in 1..n-1
CHECK     if a[read] != a[write-1]
UPDATE      a[write] = a[read]; write++
RETURN  write
```

stages.title: Reference C++
Edge cases and complexity
stages.body:
✍️ O(n) time, O(1) space.
✍️ Return the **count** `write`, not `write − 1`.
- Empty input is excluded by constraints, but the guard costs nothing.

stages.title: Carry forward
stages.body:
✍️ Sorted input + "seen before?" → compare with the neighbour / last kept, no set needed.
✍️ Compare against the **written** prefix (`a[write−k]`) to allow at most k copies.

stages.title: Interview follow-ups
stages.body:
- *Allow each value at most twice* (LeetCode 80): keep if `write < 2 || a[read] != a[write−2]`.
- *Unsorted input?* Then you need a hash set (O(n) space) or sorting first.
- *Return the count of duplicates removed.* n − k.

siblings.title: Remove Duplicates from Sorted Array II
siblings.maps: Same template, but compare with a[write−2] to allow two copies.
siblings.note:
• At most 2 copies: keep if write < 2 || a[read] ≠ a[write−2]
• Compare with the **written** array, not the input

stages.title: Analyse
stages.body:
✍️ Sorted; keep each value at most twice, in place; return k.
✍️ Trap: comparing with a[read−1] or a[read−2] (the input) fails once you start overwriting. Compare with the **written** array.

stages.title: Brainstorm
stages.body: ✍️ Counting runs works but is fiddly. Cleanest: keep a[read] if fewer than 2 elements are written, or if a[read] differs from the element written two places back.

stages.title: Algorithm in words
stages.body: ✍️ write = 0; for each element: if write < 2 or it differs from a[write−2], write it.

stages.title: Pseudocode
stages.body:
```
write = 0
for read in 0..n-1:
    if write < 2 or a[read] != a[write-2]: a[write] = a[read]; write++
return write
```

stages.title: Reference C++
Quick theory
stages.body: ✍️ "At most k copies" in a sorted array → keep if `write < k || a[read] != a[write−k]` ([[arr-read-write-pointer#variations]]).

siblings.title: Merge Sorted Array
siblings.maps: Write pointer again — but from the **back**, so nothing unread is overwritten.

stages.title: Analyse
stages.body: ✍️ nums1 has m elements plus n empty slots at the end; merge nums2 (n elements) into it, sorted, in place.

stages.title: Brainstorm
stages.body: ✍️ Merging from the front overwrites unread elements of nums1. From the back, the free slots are exactly where the largest elements go. Two read pointers (i = m−1, j = n−1), one write pointer (k = m+n−1).

stages.title: Algorithm in words
stages.body: ✍️ While nums2 has elements left: place the larger of nums1[i] and nums2[j] at k, move that pointer and k left.

stages.title: Pseudocode
stages.body:
```
i = m-1; j = n-1; k = m+n-1
while j >= 0:
    if i >= 0 and a[i] > b[j]: a[k--] = a[i--]
    else: a[k--] = b[j--]
```

stages.title: Reference C++
Quick theory
stages.body: ✍️ Loop until nums2 is used up; leftover nums1 elements are already in place. Merge step itself: [[sort-merge-sort#merge]].

siblings.title: Duplicate Zeros
siblings.maps: Another in-place write from the back: count where each element will land, then write right to left.

stages.title: Analyse
stages.body: ✍️ Duplicate every zero, shifting the rest right; elements pushed past the end are dropped. In place.

stages.title: Brainstorm
stages.body: ✍️ Shifting on each zero → O(n²). Instead: count zeros to know the final length, then walk backwards writing each element (twice for zeros) only if its target index is inside the array.

stages.title: Algorithm in words
stages.body: ✍️ zeros = count; walk i from n−1 down, with target j = i + zeros (zeros before i); write a[i] at j if j < n; if a[i] is 0, decrement zeros and write another 0 at j−1 if inside.

stages.title: Pseudocode
stages.body:
```
z = count of zeros
for i from n-1 down to 0:
    j = i + z
    if j < n: a[j] = a[i]
    if a[i] == 0:
        z = z - 1; if j-1 < n: a[j-1] = 0
```

stages.title: Reference C++
Quick theory
stages.body: ✍️ When writes move elements to the **right**, write from the right so you never overwrite something unread.

drill.title: Find Numbers with Even Number of Digits
drill.statement: Given a list of positive integers, count how many of them are written with an even number of decimal digits.
drill.approach: One pass; for each number count its digits (divide by 10, or check ranges 10–99, 1000–9999, …) and increment a counter if the count is even.
drill.trigger: "count how many elements satisfy …" with an independent per-element test.
drill.details:
**Task.** You get an array of positive integers. Count the numbers whose decimal representation has an even number of digits.

**Input:** an integer array `nums`. **Output:** an integer.

**Constraints:** 1 ≤ length ≤ 500; 1 ≤ `nums[i]` ≤ 10⁵.

**Example:** `[12, 345, 2, 6, 7896]` → `2`. 12 has two digits and 7896 has four; the others have an odd count.

drill.title: Richest Customer Wealth
drill.statement: A grid lists, for each customer (row), the money they hold in each bank (column). Return the largest total wealth of any single customer.
drill.pattern_name: Running sum per row + best so far
drill.approach: For each row, sum it with a running total, then update a global maximum.
drill.details:
**Task.** An m × n grid `accounts` gives, for customer i (a row), the amount they keep in bank j (a column). A customer's wealth is the total across all their banks. Return the wealth of the richest customer.

**Input:** a 2-D integer array. **Output:** an integer.

**Constraints:** 1 ≤ m, n ≤ 50; 1 ≤ `accounts[i][j]` ≤ 100.

**Example:** `[[1,5],[7,3],[3,5]]` → `10`. The totals are 6, 10 and 8.

drill.title: Element Appearing More Than 25% In Sorted Array
drill.statement: A sorted array has exactly one value that occurs in more than a quarter of the positions. Return it.
drill.approach: Duplicates are adjacent in sorted input, so track the length of the current run of equal values and return the value when the run exceeds n/4. (Clever version: check if a[i] == a[i + n/4].)
drill.trigger: "sorted" + "appears more than …" → equal values sit together, count runs.
drill.details:
**Task.** An array sorted in non-decreasing order contains exactly one value that fills more than 25% of its positions. Return that value.

**Input:** a sorted integer array `arr`. **Output:** an integer.

**Constraints:** 1 ≤ length ≤ 10⁴; 0 ≤ `arr[i]` ≤ 10⁵.

**Example:** `[1, 2, 2, 6, 6, 6, 6, 7, 10]` → `6`. It fills 4 of the 9 positions, which is more than a quarter.

drill.title: Three Consecutive Odds
drill.statement: Return true if the array contains three odd numbers in a row.
drill.approach: Streak counter that increments on odd and resets on even; return true when it reaches 3.
drill.details:
**Task.** Return true if somewhere in the array there are three odd numbers at consecutive positions, otherwise false.

**Input:** an integer array `arr`. **Output:** a boolean.

**Constraints:** 1 ≤ length ≤ 1000; 1 ≤ `arr[i]` ≤ 1000.

**Example:** `[1, 2, 34, 3, 4, 5, 7, 23, 12]` → `true` (5, 7, 23). `[2, 6, 4, 1]` → `false`.

drill.title: Remove One Element to Make the Array Strictly Increasing
drill.statement: Decide whether deleting exactly one element can leave the array strictly increasing.
drill.approach: Walk once counting positions where a[i] ≤ a[i−1]. More than one → false. At the single violation, check whether removing a[i−1] or a[i] fixes it by comparing with a[i−2] / a[i+1].
drill.trigger: "remove one element" + "strictly increasing" → scan once for the violation, decide locally.
drill.details:
**Task.** Remove exactly one element from the array. Can the remaining elements, in their original order, be strictly increasing? (An array that is already strictly increasing also counts: removing any one element keeps it so.)

**Input:** an integer array `nums`. **Output:** a boolean.

**Constraints:** 2 ≤ length ≤ 1000; 1 ≤ `nums[i]` ≤ 1000.

**Example:** `[1, 2, 10, 5, 7]` → `true`: remove 10 to get `[1, 2, 5, 7]`. `[2, 3, 1, 2]` → `false`. `[1, 1, 1]` → `false`.

core.subject: OOP
core.title: Classes, objects and their memory · Constructors and destructors
core.explain: An interviewer asks: "What exactly happens in memory when you write `Account a(100);` and when `a` goes out of scope?" Answer in 2 minutes: object layout, constructor call, stack vs heap, destructor call.

intro.title: Today
intro.body:
OOP is the first CS subject because every LLD round and many C++ questions sit on top of it. Today: what an object actually is in memory, and how it is born and destroyed.
✍️ Read topic 1 → write its note → answer its recall questions. Then topic 2. Then the MCQs and the 2-minute explanation.

mcqs.q: In C++, what is the only difference between `struct` and `class`?

options.b: struct members and base classes are public by default; class ones are private
options.c: struct objects live on the stack, class objects on the heap

mcqs.why: Both can have functions, constructors, inheritance and live anywhere. Only the default access differs.

mcqs.q: `class A { char c; int x; };` — on a typical 64-bit compiler, `sizeof(A)` is most likely:
mcqs.why: 1 byte for c, 3 bytes of padding so the int is 4-byte aligned, 4 bytes for x → 8.

mcqs.q: What does `sizeof` of a class with no data members return?
mcqs.why: Every object must have a distinct address, so an empty class has size 1.

mcqs.q: In which order are members initialised?

options.a: The order they appear in the initialiser list
options.c: The order they are declared in the class

mcqs.why: Declaration order always wins; compilers warn (-Wreorder) when the initialiser list order differs.

mcqs.q: `Derived` inherits from `Base`. Creating and destroying a `Derived` object calls, in order:
mcqs.why: Construction goes base → derived; destruction is the exact reverse.

mcqs.q: Which members MUST be set in the constructor initialiser list (not in the body)?
mcqs.why: const and reference members cannot be assigned after construction, so they must be initialised in the list.

micro.title: Day 1 — one pass, a few variables, and writing in place

sections.title: Today in one minute
sections.body:
Day 1 is about **not looking back**. Two ideas, four easy problems, and the habits you will use for the next 29 days.

✍️ **Running state** — walk once, keep a few variables that summarise the past.
✍️ **Read/write pointer** — one index reads everything, another marks where the next kept element goes.

The reading path below takes about 20 minutes (longer than usual — it includes the foundations). Every page opens inside the path; when you finish a step you continue from here.

sections.title: Pattern card
sections.body:
✍️ RUNNING STATE — trigger: "so far / running / streak / consecutive". Keep: total, current, best. Update every step; reset when the condition breaks.
✍️ READ/WRITE POINTER — trigger: "in-place", "O(1) extra space", "remove/move, keep order". `if keep(a[read]) a[write++] = a[read]`. Return `write`.
